entries.label: Calls every angle wider than a right angle obtuse
entries.description: The student knows an obtuse angle is wider than a right angle but forgets that it must also be smaller than a straight angle, so a straight angle or a reflex angle gets called obtuse.
entries.signal: Answers obtuse angle for a straight line, for an angle of $180^{\circ}$, or for an angle of $210^{\circ}$.

refutation.text_md: You are right that an obtuse angle is wider than a right angle. What is missing is the upper limit: an obtuse angle must also be smaller than a straight angle.
An obtuse angle is bigger than $90^{\circ}$ and smaller than $180^{\circ}$. An angle of exactly $180^{\circ}$ is a straight angle: its two sides make one straight line.
Once an angle is bigger than $180^{\circ}$ it is a reflex angle. So an angle of $210^{\circ}$ is a reflex angle, not an obtuse angle, even though it is also wider than a right angle.

Check the size against $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$ in turn. Less than $90^{\circ}$ is acute, exactly $90^{\circ}$ is right, between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$ is obtuse, exactly $180^{\circ}$ is straight, and more than $180^{\circ}$ is reflex.

verdict.reason: Real error for this objective: the straight-line figure, 180 degrees and 210 degrees all give a wide angle that is not obtuse. The ranges in the refutation (obtuse between 90 and 180, straight exactly 180, reflex over 180) match the canonical answers (straight, straight, reflex). It answers this error, since it grants the 'wider than a right angle' half and supplies the missing upper limit. It has no question ids, figure references or review history. Signal is accurate.

entries.label: Rounds an angle to the nearest right or straight angle
entries.description: The student sees an angle that is close to $90^{\circ}$ or close to a straight line and names it a right angle or a straight angle, instead of checking whether it is exactly that size.

refutation.text_md: You noticed how close the angle is to $90^{\circ}$ (or to a straight line), and comparing with those sizes is the right habit. The slip is treating "close to" as "equal to".
A right angle is exactly $90^{\circ}$, and a straight angle is exactly $180^{\circ}$. An angle that is even one degree more or less is a different type.
An angle of $91^{\circ}$ is bigger than $90^{\circ}$ and smaller than $180^{\circ}$, so it is an obtuse angle, not a right angle.
In the same way, $210^{\circ}$ is more than $180^{\circ}$, so it is a reflex angle, not a straight angle. And two sides that bend, even slightly, do not make a straight line.
So ask two questions: is it exactly $90^{\circ}$? Is it exactly $180^{\circ}$? If not, decide whether it is less than or more than each of them, and name it from that.

verdict.reason: The core error is real: a near-90 angle (91 degrees) is called right, and a nearly flat bent angle is called straight. The refutation is mathematically correct and matches the canonical answers (91 degrees is obtuse, 210 degrees is reflex). It argues against the error, 'close to' treated as 'equal to', and not only the method. It has no q: ids, figure references or review history. The signal's clause 'straight angle for 210 degrees' is not a near-miss: 210 is 30 degrees past straight, so that answer is more likely straight/reflex confusion than rounding. The signal would therefore sometimes misdiagnose, hence signal_ok false.

entries.label: Names the angle on the unmarked side of the arc
entries.description: The student names the smaller angle between the two lines, on the inside of the bend, instead of the angle the arc actually marks, so a marked reflex angle is called obtuse.
entries.signal: Answers obtuse angle when the arc is drawn round the outside of the bend.

refutation.text_md: Two lines that meet at a point make two angles, one on the inside of the bend and one on the outside. You named the inside one, which really is the smaller angle. The question, though, is about the angle the arc marks.
The arc shows which angle to name. When it is drawn round the outside of the bend, going the long way from one line to the other, the angle it marks is the larger one.
That larger angle is bigger than a straight angle, so it is more than $180^{\circ}$. An angle of more than $180^{\circ}$ is a reflex angle.

Next time, trace the arc with your finger from one line to the other. If it goes the long way round, past a straight line, the angle is a reflex angle. If it stays on the inside, name it by comparing its size with $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$.

verdict.reason: In the reflex-angle figure the arc goes round the outside of the bend, and the unmarked inside angle is about 124 degrees, obtuse. A student who names the inside angle answers obtuse. The refutation is correct: the arc picks the angle, going the long way round gives more than 180 degrees, and more than 180 degrees is reflex. It matches the canonical answer, 'Reflex angle'. It argues against the specific error and does not just restate the method, it uses no outside facts, and it has no ids or figure numbers. The signal describes the observable answer accurately.

entries.label: Swaps the names acute and obtuse
entries.description: The student judges correctly that one angle is narrow and another is wide, but attaches the names the wrong way round, calling a wide angle acute and a narrow angle obtuse.

refutation.text_md: You have judged the size correctly: one angle is narrow and the other is wide. It is the names that have been swapped, which is easy to do with two names you have to remember.

Compare with a right angle. An acute angle is narrower than a right angle, so it is smaller than $90^{\circ}$. An obtuse angle is wider than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle, so it is between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$.
For example, an angle of $91^{\circ}$ is wider than a right angle, so it is obtuse. Calling it acute would mean it is smaller than $90^{\circ}$.
Before naming an angle, ask one question: is it narrower or wider than a right angle? Narrower is acute. Wider, but not as wide as a straight line, is obtuse.

entries.label: Calls lines parallel because they look it
entries.description: The student answers 'parallel' because the lines look parallel in the picture, or because the angles come out close, even though the angle test does not hold exactly.
entries.signal: Writes that the angles are 'about' or 'nearly' equal, or 'close to' $180^\circ$, and answers parallel.

refutation.text_md: You went by how the lines look, or by the angles coming out close, and called them parallel. That is a natural first reaction, and it was right to look at the angles. The catch is that a drawing can look parallel when it is not.

The test is exact: two lines are parallel only if corresponding angles are equal, alternate interior angles are equal, or co-interior angles add up to exactly $180^\circ$. An angle that misses by a few degrees fails the test, and a few degrees is too small to see in a picture.

For example, co-interior angles of $115^\circ$ and $55^\circ$ add to $115^\circ+55^\circ=170^\circ$. That is not $180^\circ$, so those lines are not parallel, however close they look. In the same way, corresponding angles of $56^\circ$ and $45^\circ$ are not equal, so those lines are not parallel either.

Choose one pair (corresponding, alternate interior or co-interior), find both sizes (using angles on a straight line where you need to), and run the exact test. Answer 'parallel' only when the test holds exactly.

verdict.reason: Checked against the canonical solutions and the figures. The refutation's maths is correct. For the 115/55 pair, 115+55=170, which is not 180, so the lines are not parallel; this matches the book's co-interior working. For the 56/45 pair, 180-124=56, which is not equal to 45, so the lines are not parallel; this also matches the book's corresponding-angle working. Both final answers are 'not parallel', as in the book. It uses only the book's tests and the straight-line fact, and it names no question id, page or figure. It argues against this error: it says the test is exact and a drawing can mislead. It does more than restate the method. The book offers no caution on this error, so it rests on the distractors and the near-miss values (170 vs 180) in the canonical solutions. Weak spots: 'a few degrees is too small to see' sits awkwardly beside the 10-15 degree gaps in the book's own figures, and 'it was right to look at the angles' assumes the student did. Neither is wrong or harmful, so I confirm, but the first attachment fits better than the second.

entries.label: Compares the marked angles without matching their positions
entries.description: The student sets the two angle sizes marked on the figure side by side, sees that they differ, and calls the lines not parallel, without first finding the angle that sits in the matching position.

refutation.text_md: You compared the two marked angle sizes, $95^\circ$ and $85^\circ$, saw that they are different, and decided the lines are not parallel. Comparing angle sizes is the right test. The trouble is that these two are not the pair the test asks about.

The test only works on a matching pair: corresponding angles or alternate interior angles (which must be equal), or co-interior angles (which must add to $180^\circ$). Two angles in different positions can differ whether or not the lines are parallel, so their being different tells you nothing.

Here the $95^\circ$ is below the upper line, on the left of the transversal (the line cutting across), and the $85^\circ$ is below the lower line, on the right of it. They are not in matching positions. Use angles on a straight line to reach the matching one: next to the $95^\circ$ is $180^\circ-95^\circ=85^\circ$, which sits below the upper line on the right of the transversal, in the same position as the marked $85^\circ$ at the lower line. Those are corresponding angles, and they are equal.

Before you compare, ask where each angle sits at its own crossing. If it is not in the matching position, use angles on a straight line to move to the one that is, then test. Here the corresponding angles are equal, so the lines are parallel.

entries.label: Adds the squares even when a shorter side is the unknown
entries.description: The student writes $x^2 = a^2 + b^2$ with the two given lengths every time, without checking whether the unknown side is the one opposite the right angle.
entries.signal: An unknown shorter side that comes out longer than the given side opposite the right angle, for example about 13.93 instead of 12 when the given sides are 13 cm and 5 cm.

refutation.text_md: You added the two squares, which is exactly right when $x$ is the side opposite the right angle. The theorem of Pythagoras has a fixed shape, though: the square of the side opposite the right angle stands alone on one side, and the squares of the other two sides are added on the other.

Try it on a right-angled triangle where the side opposite the right angle is 13 cm and another side is 5 cm. Adding gives $x^2 = 13^2 + 5^2 = 194$. Now check that against the theorem: the squares of the two sides next to the right angle should add up to $13^2 = 169$, but $194 + 5^2 = 219$. The answer fails its own check.
Put the side opposite the right angle on its own: $13^2 = x^2 + 5^2$. Then $x^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 144$, so $x = 12$ cm, and now $144 + 25 = 169$ checks.

Before you add or subtract, find the right-angle mark and ask which side is opposite it. If $x$ is that side, add the squares of the other two, as with 15 and 20 giving $x^2 = 625$ and $x = 25$. If $x$ is one of the other two sides, subtract the square of the known short side from the square of the side opposite the right angle.

verdict.reason: I checked the figures. In the 13/5/x triangle the 13 cm side is opposite the right angle, so x^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 144 and x = 12, as the book has it. The student's sum gives 194, which is about 13.93 and longer than the 13 cm side opposite the right angle. The refutation's check also works: 194 + 25 = 219, not 169. Its example of 15 and 20 giving x^2 = 625 and x = 25 matches the book's worked answer. It argues against the error and not just the method, and uses only the book's Pythagoras method. It names no question id, page or figure, and the 15/20 example is self-contained.

entries.label: Uses only one of the two equal angles in the angle sum
entries.description: In an isosceles triangle the student knows two angles are equal but writes the angle sum with only one of them, so the unknown angle comes out too big.
entries.signal: Each equal angle comes out as 144 degrees when the angle between the two equal sides is 36 degrees, or 45 degrees when the three angles are $x$, $x$ and $3x$.

refutation.text_md: You spotted that two angles of the isosceles triangle are equal, which is the right start. The slip is in the sum of the angles: a triangle has three angles, so an equal angle has to be written twice, once for each corner it belongs to.

Take an isosceles triangle where the angle between the two equal sides is $36^{\circ}$ and the other two angles are both $x$. Writing $36^{\circ} + x = 180^{\circ}$ gives $x = 144^{\circ}$, and that angle appears at two corners. Check: $36^{\circ} + 144^{\circ} + 144^{\circ} = 324^{\circ}$, far more than the $180^{\circ}$ the angles of a triangle add up to.

With both equal angles in the sum, $180^{\circ} = 36^{\circ} + 2x$, so $2x = 144^{\circ}$. The $144^{\circ}$ is the two equal angles together, so it has to be shared between them: $x = 72^{\circ}$, and $36^{\circ} + 72^{\circ} + 72^{\circ} = 180^{\circ}$ checks.

Write one angle per corner in the sum, and let the equal angles appear as many times as there are equal corners. For angles $x$, $x$ and $3x$ that is $x + x + 3x = 180^{\circ}$, so $5x = 180^{\circ}$ and $x = 36^{\circ}$.

verdict.reason: In the figure, equal-side ticks are on NO and PO, so the 36 degree angle at O lies between the equal sides and x = y. The book's answer is 72, and the 36 degree figure with x, x, 3x gives x = 36, which the refutation reproduces. Writing 36 + x = 180 gives 144, and 36 + 144 + 144 = 324 is a valid contradiction. Writing 180 = 36 + 2x gives 2x = 144 and x = 72, which is correct and fixes the book's sign typo. Writing x + 3x = 180 gives 45, which matches the signal. The refutation is mathematically right and self-contained, uses the book's angle-sum method, and names no unseen figure or question id. One caveat is that an answer of 144 could also come from forgetting to halve 2x = 144. Step 3 covers that case too, since it says the 144 is shared between the two angles, so I do not count it as misdiagnosis.

entries.label: Treating the angles at a meeting point as vertically opposite when the lines are not straight
entries.description: The student sees two triangles touching at a point, assumes the angles there are equal because they are vertically opposite, and uses that angle as the included angle for SAS, even though the lines through the point are not straight lines.

refutation.text_md: You have two pairs of equal sides meeting at a point, and you went looking for the angle between them. That is the right instinct for SAS. The catch is the claim that the angles at that point are equal: vertically opposite angles are only equal when two **straight** lines cross.

If the sides on either side of the point do not carry on in a straight line through it, they are just sides that happen to meet there. The angles between them are not vertically opposite, and nothing given says they are equal, so you cannot use them.
Without that angle, what you really know is two equal sides in each triangle and nothing more. The book says we need at least three facts about the triangles, and two equal sides is only two facts.

Before you write "vertically opposite angles", check that both lines really are straight through the point. If you cannot show that, use only the facts you are given. If they do not complete one of SSS, SAS, AAS or RHS, the answer is "not enough information".

verdict.reason: The error is real. The book remark on the 6c pair says the lines through the shared point are not straight, so vertically opposite angles cannot be used. I checked the figure: B-C-D and A-C-E are visibly bent. The refutation matches the canonical answer (not enough information; two pairs of equal sides, fewer than three facts). It argues against the specific slip, giving the straight-lines condition and a check to run. It cites no question id, page or review history. Minor wording flaw: step 3 says 'two equal sides in each triangle', which should read 'two pairs of equal sides', but the sense is clear from step 1 and it follows the book's own phrasing.

entries.label: Treating "not enough information" as "not congruent"
entries.description: The student cannot complete a congruence rule from the facts given, or sees sides with different marks, and concludes the triangles are not congruent, as if a missing fact were proof that they differ.
entries.signal: Answers "not congruent" because no congruence rule can be completed from the facts given, or because the sides carry different marks.

refutation.text_md: You are right that nothing given lets you show these triangles are congruent: no rule from SSS, SAS, AAS and RHS is complete. The slip is the next step. Failing to show that triangles are congruent is not the same as showing that they are not.

"Not enough information" says the facts you have been given leave the question open. We cannot say they are congruent, and we cannot say they are not, because the facts that would settle it have not been given. That is the answer the book gives when a pair of triangles is in this position.

Take two isosceles triangles where the marks only show that two sides **within** each triangle are equal. Take a kite $ABCD$ with $AD=AB$ and $CD=CB$, and let the diagonals meet at $O$. Diagonal $AC$ lies between the equal sides, so it bisects $\hat{A}$: $B\hat{A}O=D\hat{A}O$. Whenever you doubt this property, check it the same way: mark the equal sides, bisect the angle between them, prove the two small triangles congruent, and use the angle sum to show the angle at the crossing point is $t+p=90^\circ$.

dropped.label: Assuming any line across a triangle is parallel to the third side
dropped.reason: The error itself is real and supported. ex7-7-4 has a bare line RP across a triangle with no tick marks, and the book's option A "parallel lines" is the wrong answer a student would pick. The canonical solution says PR is not parallel to TS because it does not bisect TQ and SQ. The refutation goes further than the book in two places, and the second is mathematically false as a general rule. Step 2 says the theorem covers "one special kind of line only", which implies that only the line joining mid-points can be parallel to the third side. Step 5 states a rule: "If not [both mid-points], there are no parallel lines to name." Step 3 draws the same conclusion from "no reason" to parallel. A line that cuts both sides in the same ratio, such as at the one-third points, is parallel to the third side without joining mid-points. The book only says the lines are not parallel according to the mid-point theorem. It never claims that failing the mid-point test makes a line non-parallel. A student who learns the step 5 rule would learn a false general principle, and under the 'when in doubt, do not confirm' standard this entry must be dropped. The other steps are consistent with the canonical solution and use no q: ids, page numbers, figure numbers or review history. In step 3, "Nothing makes either of them the mid-point" is the same claim the book's solution makes.

entries.label: Puts the factor of 2 on the wrong segment
entries.description: The student compares the right two segments but uses the 2:1 ratio the wrong way round: doubling the line joining the mid-points when it should be halved from the third side, or halving the third side when it should be doubled.
entries.signal: The answer is four times too big or four times too small, as if the long and short segments had swapped places.

refutation.text_md: You picked the right two segments to compare: the line joining the mid-points of two sides, and the third side of the triangle. The slip is in which of the two is the long one, so the factor of 2 ended up on the wrong segment.

The mid-point theorem says the line joining the mid-points is half the length of the third side. Said the other way round, the third side is twice as long as that line, a ratio of $2:1$. The third side is the long one and the line inside the triangle is the short one.

Check it with a case. If the third side is $6$ and the line joining the mid-points is $x$, then $6=2x$, so $x=\tfrac12\times 6=3$. Doubling instead would give $12$, a line inside the triangle that is longer than the side it is half of, which cannot be right.

It works the same the other way. If the line joining the mid-points is $3$ and you need the third side, then third side $=2\times 3=6$. Halving would give $1.5$, a third side shorter than the line inside it.

Before you calculate, write it as $\text{third side}=2\times(\text{line joining the mid-points})$ and put the given length in the right place. Then solve, and check that the third side comes out bigger than the line inside.

verdict.reason: The error is real and the book's own remarks stress which segment is twice as long as which (MN = 2 x PR, PR is half of MN), so the slip is plausible and supported. I worked every claim. If the third side is 6, 6 = 2x gives x = 3, and doubling gives 12, which is four times too big. If the mid-line is 3, the third side is 2 x 3 = 6, and halving gives 1.5, which is four times too small. This matches the canonical method (third side = 2 x mid-line, then solve) and the final answers. The refutation argues against this slip rather than restating the method, adds only a size sanity check that follows directly from the 2:1 ratio, and cites no question id, page, figure or review history. The signal (four times too big or too small) is accurate and specific. The description wording is a little loose but readable.

dropped.label: Uses the mid-point theorem on a segment that does not join mid-points
dropped.reason: The error is real, since the non-parallel trap question exists in this objective, and steps 1, 2 and 4 are sound. They match the book's converse reasoning that a parallel segment half the third side means its end points are mid-points. Step 3 is the problem. It tells the student 'the book's conclusion is that the mid-point theorem cannot apply, so the question has no solution'. That cites 'the book' as an authority the student cannot see. It also presents 'theorem does not apply' as 'no solution', which is false as a general rule: other methods can solve such figures, for example similar triangles for a parallel segment that is not a mid-line, as in another question of this same objective. I checked the trap figure itself, and the cosine rule gives a consistent triangle, so a student could be taught a false rule. Step 4's wording ('say the theorem does not apply') would have been safe. With the doubt on both points, it is not confirmed.
